newsitem.title: MOROCCO: Branson lifts off for round-world balloon adventure. [CORRECTED 18:40 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Branson lifts off for round-world balloon adventure. [CORRECTED 18:40 GMT]

text.p: British tycoon Richard Branson and two co-pilots soared slowly into the Moroccan sky on Tuesday, hoping to become the first to fly all around the world by balloon.

"We are now going on a great adventure. I am confident," Branson told reporters before embracing his wife Joan and children Holly and Sam and climbing into the capsule of Virgin Global Challenger for the 11.19 a.m. (1119 GMT) launch from an airbase near the Moroccan city of Marrakesh.

As the huge, white balloon with a volume of 1.1 million cubic feet (30,000 cubic metres) floated slowly upwards against a backdrop of the snowcapped Atlas Mountains, Branson could be seen waving to his family.
Co-pilot Per Lindstrand, 48, told reporters before entering the capsule: "I feel fine for the trip. Branson is getting excited."

He said the hot air and helium balloon -- as tall as a 12-storey building -- would travel at 30 to 40 km per hour (19 to 25 mph) over the Atlas Mountains and that they expected to cross the Algerian border after 12 hours.
"When we reach the jet stream our speed will accelerate," he said.

Flying eastward in the southern jet stream, Branson, Linstrand, and Alex Ritchie, 50, will head at around 30,000 feet (10,000 metres) across North Africa, Saudi Arabia and India, the South China Sea, the Pacific, United States and hopefully to touchdown in Oxfordshire in England.

"I am enjoying the best experience of my life. I am confident, I am optimistic," said Branson, the flamboyant 46-year-old head of the Virgin group of companies whose products range from condoms to cola and include an airline.
A planned dawn takeoff was delayed by the complexities of inflating the giant balloon.
Co-pilot Rory McCarthy, who was to have made up the trio of balloonists, told reporters he had to pull out because of suspected pneumonia. He was replaced by Ritchie, 50.
The weather in Marrakesh, chosen as an ideal spot to enter the southern jet stream, was reported to be perfect.
Branson expects the trip to take 14 to 21 days, with what he termed "a realistic time" of 18 days.
Branson is racing against American balloonist Steve Fosset who is planning a launch from St. Louis, Missouri, in the United States.
"I am aware of the competition but I can assure you that we will be one or two days ahead of Steve Fosset," Branson said.
Branson had to cancel a previous attempt to circumnavigate the globe from Marrakesh last January because of bad weather. He has already crossed the Atlantic and Pacific by balloon.
According to the Guinness Book of Records the furthest flown by a manned balloon is 8,382 km (5,208 miles), set by American Ben Abruzzo and three co-pilots in 1981 from Japan to California.
